claim: Complete and robust human genome duplication requires loading minichromosome maintenance (MCM) helicase complexes at many DNA replication origins.
source: Complete and robust human genome duplication requires loading minichromosome maintenance (MCM) helicase complexes at many DNA replication origins, an essential process termed origin licensing.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about DNA replication.

claim: Origin licensing is restricted to G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: Licensing is restricted to G1 phase of the cell cycle, but G1 length varies widely among cell types.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell cycle biology, stated in the abstract.

claim: G1 length varies widely among cell types.
source: Licensing is restricted to G1 phase of the cell cycle, but G1 length varies widely among cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Pluripotent stem cells with naturally short G1 phases load MCM much faster than their isogenic differentiated counterparts with long G1 phases.
source: Using quantitative single-cell analyses, we found that pluripotent stem cells with naturally short G1 phases load MCM much faster than their isogenic differentiated counterparts with long G1 phases.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During the earliest stages of differentiation toward all lineages, MCM loading slows concurrently with G1 lengthening.
source: During the earliest stages of differentiation toward all lineages, MCM loading slows concurrently with G1 lengthening, revealing developmental control of MCM loading.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Ectopic Cyclin E overproduction uncouples short G1 from fast MCM loading.
source: In contrast, ectopic Cyclin E overproduction uncouples short G1 from fast MCM loading.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Rapid licensing in stem cells is caused by accumulation of the MCM loading protein, Cdt1.
source: Rapid licensing in stem cells is caused by accumulation of the MCM loading protein, Cdt1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Prematurely slowing MCM loading in pluripotent cells lengthens G1.
source: Prematurely slowing MCM loading in pluripotent cells not only lengthens G1 but also accelerates differentiation.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Prematurely slowing MCM loading in pluripotent cells accelerates differentiation.
source: Prematurely slowing MCM loading in pluripotent cells not only lengthens G1 but also accelerates differentiation.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Rapid origin licensing is an intrinsic characteristic of stem cells that contributes to pluripotency maintenance.
source: Thus, rapid origin licensing is an intrinsic characteristic of stem cells that contributes to pluripotency maintenance.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: MCM is the core component of the replicative helicase.
source: MCM is the core component of the replicative helicase, and the process of MCM loading is termed origin licensing.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA replication.

claim: Total MCM levels remain constant throughout the cell cycle.
source: Total MCM levels remain constant throughout the cell cycle, but the levels of DNA-loaded MCM change as cells progress through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 1b and citations (Todorov et al., 1995).

claim: Cells can begin MCM loading as early as telophase and loading continues throughout G1 until the G1/S transition.
source: Cells can begin MCM loading as early as telophase and loading continues throughout G1 until the G1/S transition, the point of maximum DNA-loaded MCM (Kimura et al., 1994; Todorov et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Throughout S phase, individual MCM complexes are activated for DNA unwinding as origins 'fire'.
source: Throughout S phase, individual MCM complexes are activated for DNA unwinding as origins 'fire'.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge supported by citations (Deegan and Diffley, 2016; Remus and Diffley, 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claim: MCM complexes travel with replication forks and are progressively unloaded as replication forks terminate.
source: MCM complexes travel with replication forks and are progressively unloaded as replication forks terminate (Figure 1a) (Deegan and Diffley, 2016; Remus and Diffley, 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction, illustrated in Figure 1a, and supported by citations.

claim: Individual G1 cells have a very broad range of DNA-loaded MCM levels with a more than 100-fold difference between minimum and maximum.
source: Interestingly, individual G1 cells (blue stripe) have a very broad range of DNA-loaded MCM levels with a more than 100-fold difference between minimum and maximum (Figure 1b, left).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: MCMs are unloaded during S phase, ending in G2/M with undetectable MCM on DNA.
source: MCMs are unloaded during S phase, ending in G2/M with undetectable MCM on DNA (Figure 1b, left).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: Loaded MCM is resistant to extraction in high-salt buffer which removes peripherally bound chromatin proteins.
source: Moreover, loaded MCM is resistant to extraction in high-salt buffer which removes peripherally bound chromatin proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2f–h), similar to yeast MCM complexes loaded in vitro (Bowers et al., 2004; Randell et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2f–h and supported by citations.

claim: Loaded MCM complexes are extremely stable on DNA, both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Loaded MCM complexes are extremely stable on DNA, both in vivo and in vitro (Cocker et al., 1996; Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009; Bowers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: In human cells, MCMs can persist on DNA for more than 24 hr during a cell cycle arrest and are typically only unloaded during S phase.
source: In human cells, MCMs can persist on DNA for more than 24 hr during a cell cycle arrest and are typically only unloaded during S phase (Kuipers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: MCM loading occurs unidirectionally throughout G1 phase.
source: These properties result in MCM loading that occurs unidirectionally throughout G1 phase (Symeonidou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: G1 cells with low MCM levels are in early G1, and G1 cells with high MCM levels are in late G1.
source: The unidirectional nature of MCM loading means that G1 cells with low MCM levels are in early G1, and G1 cells with high MCM levels are in late G1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unidirectional nature of MCM loading.

claim: RPE1-hTERT cells load MCM relatively slowly during their ~ 9 hr G1.
source: Since we observed a broad distribution of MCM loading throughout G1 including many cells with low levels of loaded MCM, we conclude that RPE1-hTERT cells load MCM relatively slowly during their ~ 9 hr G1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: H9 human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) have a short G1 phase and spend most of the cell cycle in S phase.
source: H9 human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) have a short G1 phase and spend most of the cell cycle in S phase.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: The majority (~80%) of G1 hESCs had high levels of loaded MCM; very few G1 cells had low levels of loaded MCM.
source: In contrast to the differentiated epithelial cells, the majority (~80%) of G1 hESCs had high levels of loaded MCM; very few G1 cells had low levels of loaded MCM (blue cells, Figure 1d).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 1d.

claim: hESCs load MCM rapidly to achieve abundant DNA-loaded MCM in a short time.
source: This difference suggests that hESCs load MCM rapidly to achieve abundant DNA-loaded MCM in a short time.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1d.

claim: Differentiated NPCs had a longer doubling time and a wide distribution of DNA-loaded MCM in G1.
source: In contrast to hESCs, differentiated NPCs had a longer doubling time and a wide distribution of DNA-loaded MCM in G1 (blue cells, Figure 1d)
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 1d.

claim: NPCs spend approximately five time longer in G1 than hESCs.
source: they also spend approximately five time longer in G1 (Figure 1e; e.g. 15% of a 17 hr hESC cell cycle is 2.5 hr in G1 vs 45% of a 30 hr NPC cell cycle is 13.6 hr in G1).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data presented in Figure 1e.

claim: Differentiated NPCs load MCM more slowly than hESCs.
source: Since the NPCs had many cells with low levels of DNA-loaded MCM, we conclude that these differentiated cells load MCM more slowly than hESCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1d.

claim: ARPE-19-iPSCs had hallmark features of pluripotency as measured by microscopy, bisulfite sequencing, gene expression, and teratoma formation.
source: The iPSCs had hallmark features of pluripotency as measured by microscopy, bisulfite sequencing, gene expression, and teratoma formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: iPSCs G1 phases were typically seven times shorter than their differentiated parents.
source: and their G1 phases were typically seven times shorter than their differentiated parents (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1e.

claim: Pluripotent iPSCs had predominantly high levels of DNA-loaded MCM in G1.
source: Like hESCs, the pluripotent iPSCs had predominantly high levels of DNA-loaded MCM in G1 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 1d.

claim: Both pluripotent cell lines reached approximately equal levels of DNA-loaded MCM at the start of S phase as their differentiated counterparts did, but in less time.
source: Importantly, both of the pluripotent cell lines reached approximately equal levels of DNA-loaded MCM at the start of S phase as their differentiated counterparts did, but in in less time (the absolute MCM loading intensities are comparable when samples are processed and analyzed with identical instrument settings).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1d.

claim: Pluripotent cells load MCMs rapidly in G1, but differentiated cells load MCMs slowly.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that pluripotent cells load MCMs rapidly in G1, but differentiated cells load MCMs slowly.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Pluripotent hESCs loaded MCM 6.5 times faster per hour than differentiated NPCs.
source: These calculations revealed that pluripotent hESCs loaded MCM 6.5 times faster per hour than differentiated NPCs and pluripotent iPSCs loaded MCM 3.9 times faster per hour than differentiated RPEs (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from ergodic rate analysis presented in Figure 2c.

claim: Pluripotent iPSCs loaded MCM 3.9 times faster per hour than differentiated RPEs.
source: These calculations revealed that pluripotent hESCs loaded MCM 6.5 times faster per hour than differentiated NPCs and pluripotent iPSCs loaded MCM 3.9 times faster per hour than differentiated RPEs (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from ergodic rate analysis presented in Figure 2c.

claim: Pluripotent cells with short G1 phases load MCMs significantly faster than differentiated cells with long G1 phases.
source: Thus, pluripotent cells with short G1 phases load MCMs significantly faster than differentiated cells with long G1 phases.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The MCM loading rate clearly decreased for all germ layers rapidly within the first 48 hr of initiating differentiation.
source: The MCM loading rate clearly decreased for all germ layers rapidly within the first 48 hr of initiating differentiation (Figure 3a, compare the grey histograms for undifferentiated G1 cells to the green and blue histograms).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 3a.

claim: The decrease in MCM loading rate coincided with the increase in the proportion of G1 cells for each lineage.
source: The decrease in MCM loading rate also coincided with the increase in the proportion of G1 cells for each lineage.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 3a and 3b.

claim: Within 24 hr of neuroectoderm differentiation, G1 had already lengthened and MCM loading had slowed.
source: For example, within 24 hr of neuroectoderm differentiation, G1 had already lengthened and MCM loading had slowed, but during mesoderm (BMP4) differentiation both G1 lengthening and slowed MCM loading took 48 hr (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 3a and 3b.

claim: During mesoderm (BMP4) differentiation both G1 lengthening and slowed MCM loading took 48 hr.
source: For example, within 24 hr of neuroectoderm differentiation, G1 had already lengthened and MCM loading had slowed, but during mesoderm (BMP4) differentiation both G1 lengthening and slowed MCM loading took 48 hr (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 3a and 3b.

claim: MCM loading rate is coupled to G1 length.
source: The closely coordinated changes that we universally observed during differentiation suggest that MCM loading rate is coupled to G1 length.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The rate of origin licensing by MCM loading is developmentally regulated.
source: Importantly, these results demonstrate that the rate of origin licensing by MCM loading is developmentally regulated.
evidence: This is a key conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Cyclin E1 overproduction reproducibly shortened G1 length.
source: Cyclin E1 overproduction reproducibly shortened G1 length, consistent with previous studies (Figure 4a,b) (Resnitzky et al., 1994; Ekholm-Reed et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 4a and 4b, and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: Cells overproducing Cyclin E1 not only spent less time in G1 but also began S phase with much lower amounts of loaded MCM compared to the control.
source: Strikingly, cells overproducing Cyclin E1 (designated as '↑Cyclin E1') not only spent less time in G1 but also began S phase with much lower amounts of loaded MCM compared to the control; this new subpopulation appeared in the central triangular region of the plots that is typically clear of S phase cells (Figure 4c,d orange S-MCMDNApos).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 4c and 4d.

claim: Cyclin E1 overproduction dramatically increased the proportion of MCM-low early S phase cells by sixfold from 9.9% of control S phase cells to 63.6% of ↑Cyclin E1, S phase cells.
source: Cyclin E1 overproduction dramatically increased the proportion of these MCM-low early S phase cells by sixfold from 9.9% of control S phase cells to 63.6% of ↑Cyclin E1, S phase cells (Figure 4c-e).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data presented in Figure 4c-e.

claim: The MCM loading rate did not increase to accommodate the shorter G1 in Cyclin E1 overproducing cells.
source: We also conclude that the MCM loading rate did not increase to accommodate the shorter G1 because the MCM loading pattern in G1 remained constant and the ↑Cyclin E1 cells had on average at least two-fold less DNA-loaded MCM in early S phase than control cells (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4f–h.

claim: The ↑Cyclin E, MCM-low cells incorporated significantly less EdU per unit time than MCM-high cells did (1.6 fold lower mean, 1.8 fold lower median).
source: Furthermore, the ↑Cyclin E, MCM-low cells incorporated significantly less EdU per unit time than MCM-high cells did (1.6 fold lower mean, 1.8 fold lower median), indicating that low levels of loaded MCM are insufficient for normal S phase progression (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data presented in Figure 4i.

claim: Low levels of loaded MCM are insufficient for normal S phase progression.
source: Furthermore, the ↑Cyclin E, MCM-low cells incorporated significantly less EdU per unit time than MCM-high cells did (1.6 fold lower mean, 1.8 fold lower median), indicating that low levels of loaded MCM are insufficient for normal S phase progression (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4i.

claim: Shortening G1 length without increasing MCM loading rate causes G1 cells to enter S phase prematurely without the full complement of DNA-loaded MCM.
source: Thus, shortening G1 length without increasing MCM loading rate causes G1 cells to enter S phase prematurely without the full complement of DNA-loaded MCM.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Total Mcm2 and ORC protein levels remained constant between pluripotent and differentiated cells.
source: Total Mcm2 and ORC protein levels remained constant (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Cdc6 protein levels are low in G1 and high in S phase.
source: Cdc6 protein levels are low in G1 and high in S phase (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section, illustrated in Figure 5b, and supported by a citation (Mailand and Diffley, 2005; Pozo and Cook, 2016).

claim: Cdt1 protein levels are high in G1 and low in S phase.
source: Conversely, Cdt1 protein levels are high in G1 and low in S phase (Figure 5b) (Mailand and Diffley, 2005; Pozo and Cook, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section, illustrated in Figure 5b, and supported by citations.

claim: Cdc6 was higher in pluripotent cells than in differentiated cells.
source: Cdc6 was indeed higher in pluripotent cells, as was Geminin, a protein regulated in a similar manner as Cdc6 (Figure 5a) (McGarry and Kirschner, 1998).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Geminin was higher in pluripotent cells than in differentiated cells.
source: Cdc6 was indeed higher in pluripotent cells, as was Geminin, a protein regulated in a similar manner as Cdc6 (Figure 5a) (McGarry and Kirschner, 1998).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Even though the majority of asynchronous pluripotent cells were in S phase, Cdt1 levels were higher in asynchronous pluripotent cells than in isogenic differentiated cells.
source: To our surprise, even though the majority of asynchronous pluripotent cells were in S phase, a time when Cdt1 is degraded, Cdt1 levels were higher in asynchronous pluripotent cells than in isogenic differentiated cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Cdt1 levels are higher in G1 phase of pluripotent cells than G1 of differentiated cells.
source: These data imply that Cdt1 levels are higher in G1 phase of pluripotent cells than G1 of differentiated cells, providing a potential explanation for fast MCM loading in pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: S phase Cdt1 degradation in hESCs is similar to differentiated cells with very low levels in S phase.
source: S phase Cdt1 degradation in hESCs is similar to differentiated cells with very low levels in S phase (purple, Figure 5c).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5c.

claim: hESCs had a large population of cells with high Cdt1 levels in G1 and significant amounts of Cdt1 in G2/M phase.
source: In contrast, the hESCs had a large population of cells with high Cdt1 levels in G1 (green cells) and significant amounts of Cdt1 in G2/M phase (grey cells), whereas the NPCs had a broad and overall lower Cdt1 distribution in G1 and very little Cdt1 in G2/M (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: NPCs had a broad and overall lower Cdt1 distribution in G1 and very little Cdt1 in G2/M.
source: In contrast, the hESCs had a large population of cells with high Cdt1 levels in G1 (green cells) and significant amounts of Cdt1 in G2/M phase (grey cells), whereas the NPCs had a broad and overall lower Cdt1 distribution in G1 and very little Cdt1 in G2/M (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: G1 hESCs consistently harbored significantly more Cdt1 than G1 NPCs did (2.9-fold higher median, 2.2-fold higher mean).
source: The G1 hESCs consistently harbored significantly more Cdt1 than G1 NPCs did (2.9-fold higher median, 2.2-fold higher mean, three replicates [Figure 5d]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data presented in Figure 5d.

claim: CDT1 mRNA is modestly but consistently higher in asynchronous hESCs compared to differentiated derivatives.
source: We note that CDT1 mRNA is modestly but consistently higher in asynchronous hESCs compared to differentiated derivatives, and that Cdt1 protein levels decrease during early differentiation coincident with the slowdown in licensing rate, but before loss of Oct4 (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cdt1 protein levels decrease during early differentiation coincident with the slowdown in licensing rate, but before loss of Oct4.
source: We note that CDT1 mRNA is modestly but consistently higher in asynchronous hESCs compared to differentiated derivatives, and that Cdt1 protein levels decrease during early differentiation coincident with the slowdown in licensing rate, but before loss of Oct4 (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The higher amount of Cdt1 specifically in G1 contributes to the fast MCM loading rate in hESCs.
source: We postulate that the higher amount of this essential MCM loading protein specifically in G1 contributes to the fast MCM loading rate in hESCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Cdt1 depletion reduced MCM loading rate in hESCs.
source: As expected, Cdt1 depletion reduced MCM loading rate in hESCs (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 6c.

claim: G1 length increased coincidentally with the decrease in MCM loading rate upon Cdt1 depletion in hESCs.
source: Strikingly, G1 length increased coincidentally with the decrease in MCM loading rate (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 6d.

claim: There is a close link between MCM loading rate and G1 length in hESCs.
source: These data corroborate the close link between MCM loading rate and G1 length in hESCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Inducible Cdt1 overproduction was insufficient to accelerate MCM loading in RPE cells.
source: We first constructed an RPE_hTERT derivative with ~two-fold inducible Cdt1 overproduction, but this manipulation was insufficient to accelerate MCM loading (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Ectopic myc-tagged Cdc6 expressed constitutively in RPE cells had only minimal effects on MCM loading rate.
source: We also tested ectopic myc-tagged Cdc6 expressed constitutively in RPE cells (Figure 6e); this addition also had only minimal effects on MCM loading rate (Figure 6g, compare the grey and green histograms).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 6e and 6g.

claim: Expression of the stable Cdc6-mut was sufficient to increase MCM loading rates in RPE cells.
source: Expression of the stable Cdc6-mut was sufficient to increase MCM loading rates (Figure 6g, compare the blue histogram to the grey and green histograms)
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 6g.

claim: Cdt1 overproduction had little additive effect on MCM loading rate in RPE cells expressing Cdc6-mut.
source: Cdt1 overproduction had little additive effect on MCM loading rate in RPE cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Accelerating MCM loading by expressing stable Cdc6-mut did not shorten G1 in RPEs.
source: Interestingly accelerating MCM loading by this method did not shorten G1 in RPEs (Figure 6f), further demonstrating that the length of G1 phase and the rate of MCM loading to license origins can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 6f.

claim: The length of G1 phase and the rate of MCM loading to license origins can be uncoupled.
source: Interestingly accelerating MCM loading by this method did not shorten G1 in RPEs (Figure 6f), further demonstrating that the length of G1 phase and the rate of MCM loading to license origins can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6f.

claim: Rapid MCM loading itself is not sufficient to trigger S phase entry.
source: Slow MCM loading may delay S phase entry through the licensing checkpoint (Teer et al., 2006; Shreeram et al., 2002; Nevis et al., 2009; Ge and Blow, 2009), but rapid MCM loading itself is not sufficient to trigger S phase entry.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6 and supported by citations.

claim: Stimulating control hESCs with 10 ng/mL of BMP4 slightly shifted the population toward differentiation, but most cells remained pluripotent with high Oct4 levels at 48 hours.
source: Stimulating control hESCs with 10 ng/mL of BMP4 slightly shifted the population toward differentiation, but most cells remained pluripotent with high Oct4 levels at this time point.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 7b and 7c.

claim: hESCs pretreated with Cdt1 siRNA to prematurely slow MCM loading gained a substantial population of Oct4 negative-Cdx2 positive differentiating cells relative to controls.
source: Strikingly, hESCs pretreated with Cdt1 siRNA to prematurely slow MCM loading gained a substantial population of Oct4 negative-Cdx2 positive differentiating cells relative to controls that were treated similarly.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 7b and 7c.

claim: After 10 ng/ml BMP4 treatment, Cdt1-depleted hESCs had significantly higher differentiation scores than controls (p<0.0001).
source: After 10 ng/ml BMP4 treatment, Cdt1-depleted hESCs had significantly higher scores, indicating that prematurely slowing MCM loading promoted differentiation (p<0.0001, two-tailed Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data presented in Figure 7d.

claim: Both control cells and Cdt1-depleted cells differentiated more fully at a higher concentration of 50 ng/mL BMP4, but the Cdt1-depleted cells still differentiated further than the controls (p<0.0001).
source: Both control cells and Cdt1-depleted cells differentiated more fully at a higher concentration of 50 ng/mL BMP4, but the Cdt1-depleted cells still differentiated further than the controls (p<0.0001, two-tailed Mann-Whitney test, Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data presented in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Prematurely slowing MCM loading prior to endoderm differentiation also increased the number of cells positive for the endoderm transcription factor Sox17 relative to controls.
source: Importantly, the phenotype was conserved across multiple differentiation lineages, as prematurely slowing MCM loading prior to endoderm differentiation also increased the number of cells positive for the endoderm transcription factor Sox17 relative to controls at the same time point (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Slowing licensing by depleting Cdc6 significantly promoted differentiation (p<0.0001).
source: Despite the short G1 length, slowing MCM loading by depleting Cdc6 significantly promoted differentiation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2b–f, p<0.0001, two-tailed Mann-Whitney test.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2b–f.

claim: Slow MCM loading generally promoted differentiation.
source: Thus, we conclude that slow MCM loading generally promoted differentiation and by extension, that rapid MCM loading preserves pluripotency.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 7 and supplementary figures.

claim: Rapid MCM loading preserves pluripotency.
source: Thus, we conclude that slow MCM loading generally promoted differentiation and by extension, that rapid MCM loading preserves pluripotency.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 7 and supplementary figures.

claim: Rapid MCM loading to license replication origins is an intrinsic property of pluripotent cells.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that rapid MCM loading to license replication origins is an intrinsic property of pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Human embryonic stem cells have a remarkably fast MCM loading rate.
source: Human embryonic stem cells have a remarkably fast MCM loading rate, and reprogramming to create induced pluripotent stem cells increases MCM loading rate.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Reprogramming to create induced pluripotent stem cells increases MCM loading rate.
source: Human embryonic stem cells have a remarkably fast MCM loading rate, and reprogramming to create induced pluripotent stem cells increases MCM loading rate.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: This is the first demonstration that the rate of MCM loading is developmentally regulated.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that the rate of MCM loading is developmentally regulated.
evidence: This is a claim made by the authors in the discussion.

claim: Developmental regulation of MCM loading rate is consistent with previous work showing higher levels of total Cdt1 in asynchronous mouse ESCs than in differentiated cells.
source: Developmental regulation of MCM loading rate is consistent with previous work showing higher levels of total Cdt1 in asynchronous mouse ESCs than in differentiated cells (Ballabeni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement in the discussion that connects the current findings to previous work.

claim: The regulated decrease in MCM loading rate is critical during differentiation.
source: The regulated decrease in MCM loading rate is critical during differentiation, as rapid MCM loading protects pluripotency, and prematurely slowing MCM loading promotes differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Stem cells achieve faster MCM loading, at least in part, by particularly high Cdt1 levels in G1.
source: Stem cells achieve faster MCM loading, at least in part, by particularly high Cdt1 levels in G1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: High Cdt1 levels in stem cells are achieved not only by a modest difference in CDT1 mRNA but also post-transcriptionally by specific re-accumulation of Cdt1 protein in the preceding G2 phase.
source: These high levels are achieved not only by a modest difference in CDT1 mRNA (Figure 3c) but also post-transcriptionally by specific re-accumulation of Cdt1 protein in the preceding G2 phase (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the data presented in Figures 3c and 5c.

claim: Cdt1 stability in G2 phase has been attributed to geminin-mediated protection from the SCFSkp2 E3 ubiquitin ligase in non-stem cells.
source: Cdt1 stability in G2 phase has been attributed to geminin-mediated protection from the SCFSkp2 E3 ubiquitin ligase in non-stem cells (Tsunematsu et al., 2013; Ballabeni et al., 2004; Clijsters et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement in the discussion that cites previous work.

claim: Cdt1 is protected in late S phase and G2 by cyclin A/Cdk1 activity.
